title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Resp.: negative (Scotus permissive) vs punitive reprobation — if the latter, we grant
pass_a_gloss: That all these may be washed away, first it is to be recalled to memory that we treat of that reprobation which the Theologians call negative; which Scotus calls permissive, in the Sentences book 1, distinction 41, question 1; not of that which it is permitted to call positive or punitive. The former so considered says only the eternal purpose of God concerning not granting to certain singular persons some gratuitous, unowed, and special benefit, which being granted they would be softened, converted, and infallibly led unto eternal life. The latter says the eternal purpose of God concerning certain persons to be punished with eternal death on account of those sins which they will perpetrate, and from which they are foresighted as least to be freed. If the adversaries look to this latter decree, we freely grant that this eternal decree of predamnation tends unto no one, except by that reason that he is bound by the guilt of sin. For although God wills to save the miserable without any merits of theirs, because he is good, yet he does not will to damn or punish innocents without any demerits, because he is just.
pass_b_english: To clear all this, recall first: we are treating the reprobation theologians call negative — which Scotus calls permissive (Sentences 1, dist. 41, q. 1) — not the positive or punitive kind. Negative reprobation, so taken, means only God's eternal purpose not to grant certain particular persons some gratuitous, unowed, special benefit by which, if granted, they would be softened, converted, and infallibly led to eternal life. Positive reprobation means God's eternal purpose to punish certain persons with eternal death for the sins they will commit, and from which they are foresighted as not to be freed. If adversaries mean that latter decree, we freely grant: the eternal decree of predamnation tends to no one except as bound by sin's guilt. God wills to save the miserable without their merits, because he is good; he does not will to damn or punish innocents without demerits, because he is just.
source_text: Ut haec omnia diluantur, primo in memoriam revocandum est, nos agere de reprobatione illa, quam Theologi vocant negativam; quam Scotus permissivam appellat, in Sentent. lib. 1, dist. 41, quaest. 1; non de illa quam positivam sive punitivam licet appellare. Prior ita considerata dicit solummodo Dei propositum aeternum de non-concedendo singularibus quibusdam personis gratuitum quoddam, indebitum, et speciale beneficium, quo concesso emollirentur, converterentur, et ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter perducerentur. Posterior dicit aeternum Dei propositum de quibusdam personis morte aeterna puniendis ob peccata illa quae perpetrabunt, et a quibus minime liberandi praevidentur. Si ad hoc posterius decretum respiciant adversarii, ultro largimur, hoc aeternum praedamnationis decretum non tendere in quenquam, nisi ea ratione quod peccati reatu constringatur. Nam licet Deus velit servare miseros absque ullis eorum meritis, quia bonus est, non tamen vult damnare aut punire innocentes absque ullis demeritis, quia justus est.
